Normandy
NOR-man-dee
n. (the northern province of Rouen, Caen and Dieppe, with a strong Reformed minority and the synod of Alencon of 1637)
French Normandie, the land of the Northmen, settled by Norse under Rollo from 911.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Normandy is the northern French province where the Reformed church was numerous enough to matter and never numerous enough to be safe. Rouen, Caen, Dieppe and Alencon all held substantial Reformed congregations from the 1550s, drawn from merchants, artisans, printers and a part of the gentry; Rouen was one of the eight places where a national synod of the French churches met, and Caen had a Reformed academy. The province paid in blood for it: Rouen was taken by the Catholic forces in 1562 with a sack, Augustin Marlorat its minister being hanged in the ruins of his own church; the news of the Paris massacre of August 1572 was followed by killings at Rouen, where some hundreds of Protestants were murdered in the prisons in September. The national synod that met at Alencon in 1637 is Normandy's chief theological occasion: it examined Moise Amyraut and Paul Testard of Saumur over the hypothetical universalism they taught, and let them keep their chairs on an undertaking about their manner of teaching. Elie Benoist, pastor at Alencon, wrote after the Revocation the standard history of the Edict of Nantes. The dictionary enters Normandy because Alencon's refusal to condemn Amyraut is where the French Reformed church chose to live with an unsettled doctrine of the extent of the atonement.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; atonement as expiation and satisfaction; hypothetical as conditional or supposed; and a sack as the pillage of a town.

expand to see more

SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an assembly of ministers and elders.

ATONEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury.

HYPOTHETICAL, a. Including a supposition; conditional; assumed without proof for the purpose of reasoning.

SACK, n. The pillage or plunder of a town or city; the storm and spoil of a place taken by assault.

ACADEMY, n. A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.

Key Scripture

Joh 10:15 — "As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep."

Eph 5:25 — "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;"

Joh 17:9 — "I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine."

Isa 53:11 — "He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities."

Modern Corruption

Northern province of Rouen, Caen and Dieppe, where Marlorat was hanged in 1562 and the synod of Alencon in 1637 declined to condemn Amyraut.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the universal intention of the atonement, which Amyraut taught at Saumur as a decree to save all men on condition of faith, with the effectual decree following; and the dictionary holds that this makes the Son's work wider than the Father's election and the Spirit's application, which Scripture does not. The Lord states the extent himself in the same breath as the act: “I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15), and the husband's pattern is that “Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” (Eph 5:25). Alencon in 1637 did not condemn it, and the Helvetic Consensus had to deal with it thirty-eight years later.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the definite success of the atonement, which is what makes it good news to anybody. The high priestly prayer is deliberately bounded: “I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (Joh 17:9). And the servant's satisfaction is guaranteed, not offered: “He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied” (Isa 53:11). The dictionary records that Amyraut was a serious and devout man and that Normandy's synod acted charitably toward him, and that the charity cost the French church a settled doctrine.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek probaton (G4263), a sheep; Greek ekklesia (G1577), the church; Hebrew amal (H5999), travail, toil.

expand to see more

Greek probaton (G4263) — a sheep, one of the flock; “I lay down my life for the sheep”, John 10:15.

Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out, the church; “Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it”, Ephesians 5:25.

Greek erotao (G2065) — to ask, to request; “I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me”, John 17:9.

Hebrew amal (H5999) — toil, travail, labour; “He shall see of the travail of his soul”, Isaiah 53:11.

Hebrew sabea (H7646) — to be satisfied, to be filled; “and shall be satisfied”, Isaiah 53:11.

Usage

"“I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15) — the synod of Alencon examining Amyraut in 1637."

"“I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (Joh 17:9) — a conditional decree to save all men."

"“He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied” (Isa 53:11) — Marlorat hanged in his own church at Rouen, 1562."
